sentences.text: The name Tethyshadros honors the ancient Tethys Ocean and the Hadrosauroidea group, while the species name means "insular" to reflect its island habitat.
The holotype, nicknamed "Antonio," is a mostly complete but crushed skeleton, while an additional extensive skeleton named "Bruno" was found nearby.
This animal possessed a beak, hands that formed into fleshy pads, and three-toed feet.
Scientists spent 2,800 hours removing the fossil from the rock matrix.
The subadult "Antonio" weighed approximately 338 kg, whereas the adult "Bruno" weighed between 514 and 584 kg.
Bruno was between 15% and 20% larger than Antonio and showed adult traits like a more robust skull.
A nearly complete hadrosauroid skeleton was found in 1994 at an abandoned quarry, but it was not fully extracted until 1999.
The excavation block containing the specimen weighed five tons and was too large to move as a single unit.
The genus was officially named and described by Dalla Vecchia in 2009.
Growth lines in the bones show the holotype was between 5 and 6 years old when it died.
In 2021, researchers placed Tethyshadros as the sister taxon to Fylax within the Hadrosauromorpha clade.
In 2026, Magyar and colleagues recovered Tethyshadros as the sister taxon to Kryptohadros using updated phylogenetic matrices.
Magyar et al. named the clade containing Tethyshadros, Kryptohadros, and Telmatosaurus as Telmatosauridae.
Cladistic analysis indicated that Tethyshadros was closely related to Hadrosauridae sensu Sereno and Telmatosaurus.

In 2021, Prieto-Márquez and Carrera Farias recovered Tethyshadros as the sister taxon of Fylax in a derived position within Hadrosauromorpha, making it one of the last surviving non-hadrosaurid hadrosauromorphs.
The parent group and family of Tethyshadros are both identified as Telmatosauridae.
Tethyshadros lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically the Campanian age.
This dinosaur is found in the Lipica Formation near Trieste, Italy, and was previously thought to belong to the Liburnia Formation.
The time range for Tethyshadros is the Campanian stage, from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
The total estimated body length is 4.5 meters, though some argue this figure is an overestimate.
It is debated whether the holotype represented an adult or a subadult, with later assessments based on bone histology suggesting it was a subadult.
Dalla Vecchia rejected the possibility that the species was a remnant of isolated evolution of earlier European hadrosauroids or descended from American hadrosaurids.
A 2020 description by Della Vacchia focusing on the tail anatomy was mostly refuted in subsequent studies.
